title: Two sets of cousins
hookLine: cousins under one roof, two claims to one throne, and the question of dharma
carry: dharma is what holds the house up

cards: Cousins who grew up together. Then something breaks between two sides of the family, and now at weddings they sit at opposite ends of the room. The Ramayana was about one family and an enemy outside it.
The other great epic, the Mahabharata, is about a family where the enemy is inside. Remember Ganesha breaking his tusk to keep writing? Tradition says this is the book he was writing.

teach.h: THE BLIND ELDER, THE YOUNGER KING.
teach.b: Two brothers. The elder, Dhritarashtra, was born blind, so by the rules of the time he was passed over for the throne. The younger, Pandu, became king.
Pandu's five sons are the Pandavas. Yudhishthira, the eldest, so honest it becomes a problem. Bhima, huge, hungry and strong.

Arjuna, the archer. And the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Dhritarashtra and his wife Gandhari, who bound her own eyes with a cloth for life so she'd never see more than her husband, have a hundred sons, the Kauravas.
The eldest is Duryodhana. Then Pandu dies young, and his five boys come to live in the palace at Hastinapura with their hundred cousins. It goes bad early.
Duryodhana's jealousy becomes hatred. He poisons Bhima and throws him into a river; Bhima survives.

When people start calling Yudhishthira the heir, Duryodhana talks his father into sending the Pandavas away, to a house built of lac and other things that burn, meant to be set alight with them inside.
Warned in time, they dig a tunnel, set the fire themselves, and slip away.
Whose throne is it? Duryodhana is the son of the elder brother, now on the throne. Yudhishthira is the eldest son of the king who reigned.
Both have a case. Neither lets go. This is why the Mahabharata matters so much to Hindus.
Its real subject is dharma: the right way to live, your duty to the people around you. The word comes from a root meaning to hold up.

teach.h: DHARMA: WHAT HOLDS IT ALL UP.
teach.b: Dharma is what holds a family, a kingdom, a world together. And the eldest Pandava, Yudhishthira, is called Dharmaraja, the king of dharma. The epic doesn't only ask who gets the throne.
It asks: what is dharma here, when both sides have a claim?

how: Hindus know the Mahabharata through family retellings, comic books, television serials and temple recitations; tradition names the sage Vyasa as its author and Ganesha as the scribe who wrote it down.

o: a son of Pandu: one of the five brothers
a palace guard sworn to the Kuru throne
a son of Dhritarashtra: one of the hundred

s: the Pandavas and Kauravas are strangers from rival kingdoms
they're first cousins, raised in the same palace.
Yudhishthira is called Dharmaraja, the king of dharma
and dharma, what holds a family and a world together, is what the whole epic is about.
only one side has a real claim to the throne
each side has a case: the son of the reigning elder, and the son of the king who reigned.

games.q: you're Dhritarashtra, the blind king. your son hates his cousins and the throne could go to either family. what do you do?
o: send your son away from court.
let your son have his way, again and again.
games.why: he gives in to his son and sends the Pandavas away to the house built to burn. over and over, his love for his son wins over dharma, and it helps drive the family to war.

practice: Think of a split in a family you know, two sides that used to share a table. Instead of asking who's right, ask the Mahabharata's question: what would dharma ask of me here, in my place in this family?
If you pray, hold both sides before God, by name, without picking a winner.

wordCard.voice: Pandava, son of Pandu: the name for the five brothers, growing up under one roof with their hundred Kaurava cousins and one throne between them.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Pandava, 'son of Pandu'. The five brothers are named after their father.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma is what holds the house up. Both sides grew up under one roof. Day seventy-one, done.
